books.title: The Song of the Lark
books.author: Willa Cather
books.desc: A gifted girl from a small Colorado railroad town discovers her singing voice and struggles to become a great opera singer.
about: In Moonstone, Colorado, Thea Kronborg, the daughter of a Swedish minister, is a serious and talented girl, encouraged by the kindly Doctor Archie, her piano teacher Wunsch, the Mexican musician Spanish Johnny and the railroad man Ray Kennedy, who hopes to marry her one day. She goes to Chicago to study piano with Harsanyi, who discovers that her true gift is her voice. A stay among the ancient cliff dwellings of Panther Canyon in Arizona, with her friend Fred Ottenburg, helps her understand what art means to her.

Cather's novel is a portrait of the artist as a young woman, describing the long, lonely labour behind artistic achievement, against the backdrop of the American West and fast-growing Chicago at the turn of the twentieth century.
The Song of the Lark was published in 1915. Its title and first-edition cover come from an 1884 painting by Jules Breton in the Art Institute of Chicago. This text follows the 1915 edition.

books.title: Maggie: A Girl of the Streets
books.author: Stephen Crane
books.desc: A girl growing up in a brutal New York tenement hopes to escape poverty through her love for a bartender, but finds only rejection.
about: In Rum Alley, a poor district of New York's Bowery, Maggie Johnson grows up with her violent, drunken parents and her brother Jimmie, who becomes a hardened, cynical young man. Maggie, who has somehow "blossomed in a mud puddle", falls for Jimmie's friend Pete, a swaggering bartender, believing he will help her escape the life she leads. When she goes with him, her family and neighbours turn against her.
Crane's short novel is an early work of American naturalism, a bleak and ironic portrait of slum life, hypocrisy and the forces that crush the poor, written largely in the dialect of the streets.
Crane, then 21, financed the first edition himself in 1893 under the pseudonym Johnston Smith. After the success of The Red Badge of Courage, Maggie was reissued in a revised version in 1896.

books.title: The Blithedale Romance
books.author: Nathaniel Hawthorne
books.desc: A young poet joins a utopian farming community in Massachusetts and watches the passions of three remarkable people unfold around him.
about: Miles Coverdale, a minor poet, leaves Boston to join the community of Blithedale, where idealists hope to build a better society through shared farm work. There he meets the brilliant and beautiful Zenobia, the stern reformer Hollingsworth, who is obsessed with his plan to reform criminals, and the frail, mysterious Priscilla, whom the old beggar Moodie has asked Hollingsworth to protect. The arrival of the sinister Westervelt reveals hidden links between the characters.
Told by the observant but detached Coverdale, Hawthorne's novel examines the gap between ideals and human passions, as well as reform, love and the place of women in society.
The Blithedale Romance was published in 1852. Its setting is based on Brook Farm, the utopian community of which Hawthorne was a founding member and where he lived in 1841.

books.title: The Innocents Abroad
books.author: Mark Twain
books.desc: Mark Twain joins a group of American tourists on a pleasure cruise to Europe and the Holy Land, and mocks both the Old World and his fellow travellers.
about: In 1867 Twain sails on the chartered steamship Quaker City with a party of American pilgrims and sightseers on a five-month "Great Pleasure Excursion". He describes the Azores, Gibraltar, Paris during the Exposition, Italy and Rome, a side trip through the Black Sea to Odessa, Sebastopol and Yalta, Constantinople, and finally the Holy Land and Egypt, mocking guidebooks, guides, old masters and the solemn piety of his companions.

Twain's humorous travel book combines satire, comic exaggeration and occasional moments of genuine admiration, and punctures the reverence of American tourists for Europe and the Holy Land. Its descriptions of peoples of the Middle East reflect the prejudices of its time.

The Innocents Abroad, or The New Pilgrims' Progress was published in 1869. It grew out of letters Twain wrote during the voyage for the Alta California newspaper, which paid for his trip, and became the best-selling of his books during his lifetime.

books.title: Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl
books.author: Harriet Jacobs
books.desc: Writing as "Linda Brent", a woman born into slavery in North Carolina tells how she escaped her master's harassment and hid for seven years to protect her children.
about: "Linda Brent" is born into slavery in a small town in North Carolina. Her first mistress teaches her to read and write, but at her death Linda passes into the household of Dr. Flint, who pursues her with sexual harassment while his jealous wife persecutes her. To protect herself, she has two children, Benny and Ellen, with a white neighbour, Mr. Sands. When Dr. Flint threatens to sell her children, she hides in a tiny crawlspace under the roof of her grandmother's house, where she remains for seven years before escaping to the North.

The book uses the techniques of the sentimental novel to address the sexual abuse suffered by enslaved women and their struggle to protect their children, and appeals directly to the women of the North.
Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, Written by Herself was published in 1861 under the pseudonym Linda Brent, edited by the abolitionist Lydia Maria Child. Dr. Flint is based on James Norcom.
books.author_short: African-American abolitionist and writer (1813 or 1815–1897), author of Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl.
author_long: Harriet Jacobs was born into slavery in Edenton, North Carolina, in 1813 or 1815. After years of sexual harassment by her enslaver, she hid for seven years in a crawlspace in her grandmother's house before escaping to New York in 1842. She found work as a nanny and came into contact with abolitionist and feminist reformers. She died on 7 March 1897.
Her autobiography, Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861), published under the pseudonym Linda Brent, is now considered an American classic.
